t: Confucianism grew from the teaching of Confucius, a scholar of the state of Lu who taught that a good society rests on humane, cultivated people who honour their families, observe ritual and govern by virtue.

Adopted by the Han emperors and later made the basis of the civil service examinations, it was the official orthodoxy of the Chinese empire for some two thousand years and the model of government in Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
Attacked as a cause of backwardness in the 20th century, it has revived since the 1980s, and its ideals of learning, family duty and moral government remain deeply rooted in East Asian societies.
dyk: The descendants of Confucius have kept their family records for more than eighty generations: their genealogy is often described as the longest recorded family tree in the world.
ev: Confucius is born in the state of Lu, by the traditional date
Confucius dies; his disciples gather his sayings, later compiled as the Analects
Mencius teaches that human nature is good and that rulers who oppress the people lose the mandate of Heaven
The Qin dynasty orders the burning of books, the Confucian classics among them, by the traditional account
Emperor Wu of Han establishes official chairs for the Five Classics
The Sui dynasty founds the imperial examinations, later based on the Confucian classics
Zhu Xi publishes the Four Books with his commentaries, the core of Neo-Confucianism
The Qing government abolishes the imperial examinations

f.origin: The state of Lu, in present-day Shandong, China, late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE
f.founder: Confucius (Kongzi, 551–479 BCE), with the later teachers Mencius and Xunzi
f.scriptures: The Five Classics; the Four Books: the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean
f.followers: Few people claim it as their religion, but its values of family, learning and ritual are shared by hundreds of millions across East Asia
